https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-zelenskyy-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I71E Kyiv has come under repeated Russian attacks this week Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS Advertisement At least nine people died and 23 were injured after Russia struck Ukraine 's capital city Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said on Saturday morning. The missiles struck several homes and a five-storey residential building, while cars were also set alight. Several buildings in Kyiv caught fire during the onslaught Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS What else do we know about the damage from the attack? Four children were among the 23 injured, the emergency service said. In a post on his Telegram account, Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said that several people were trapped in a damaged residential building during the attack. The first and second floors of the building had partially collapsed, he said, while some warehouses in the city were also on fire. 'Fire and destruction' affected 5 Kyiv districts, emergency services said Image: Sergei Supinsky/AFP Zelenskyy stresses need for defense systems Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched 35 missiles overnight, including 27 ballistic missiles, as well as 185 attack drones. He said only one ballistic missile was intercepted, blaming a shortage of interceptors for Ukraine's Patriot air defense systems. "As usual, the Russians struck ordinary residential buildings," Zelenskyy said, adding that 18 residential buildings, a school, the Lithuanian Embassy and infrastructure facilities were damaged. "Every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives of our people," he said. "And every night without them results in more casualties." The attacks come as Moscow has intensified its bombing campaigns in recent weeks and months. Last week, Zelenskyy met with his US counterpart Donald Trump and the UK's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham as he seeks increased support to boost Ukraine's air defences. Kyiv hits back against shipping and oil infrastructure Zelenskyy later said Ukrainian forces had responded with strikes on targets inside Russia and in the Black Sea region. "Grateful to Ukrainian warriors who are bringing the war back to Russia and responding to its attacks against life," he said, adding that Ukraine was targeting "facilities that sustain the war effort." He said Ukrainian forces had sunk the sanctioned Russian container ship Yanina and struck infrastructure at three oil refineries in Russia's Bashkortostan region, nearly 1,600 kilometers (994 miles) from Ukraine. Independent reporting confirms Zelenskyy announced both sets of strikes on Saturday. "We continue applying our just pressure," Zelenskyy said. "Our long-range sanctions plan is being implemented step by step." Subsequently, Russia's Defence Ministry said Moscow's forces had struck a fuel storage facility and oil refinery in the Ukrainian port city of Odesa. The ministry said a vessel south of the port was also hit delivering supplies for the Ukrainian military. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.southwalesargus.co.uk/news/2.text: Cardiff Airport Ryanair Leisure Travel Ryanair warns Cardiff Airport passengers of long EES queues By Patrick Glover Trending News Reporter Share 0 Comments Ryanair has issued a new warning to travellers amid ongoing disruptions caused by the EU's new Entry/Exit System (EES). (Image: Cardiff Airport) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Cardiff Airport passengers can expect lengthy delays at European airports this summer due to the EU’s new Entry/Exit System (EES). Ryanair has issued a new warning to travellers amid ongoing disruptions at 16 major airports. The EES, introduced in October last year and ramped up on April 10, requires British and other non-EU travellers to submit biometric data—fingerprints and facial scans—upon entry into the Schengen Area. The new EES has received significant backlash since its introduction, with it causing long waits for passengers at airports. Some travellers have already experienced waits of up to six hours, and industry experts warn these disruptions could continue for up to two years . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Portugal Travel Advisor | Julia T (@travel_luckk) Major airlines, including Jet2 and Ryanair, have called for the rollout of the new system to be suspended until after the summer to allow for a "smoother airport experience" during peak travel season. CEO of Malta Air, David O’Brien, even threatened to pull all flights to Malta due to the extended wait times caused by the EES at airports. Cardiff Airport passengers warned of long queues at 13 major European airports Brits heading to Europe this summer have been told to expect more delays due to the EES. Ryanair has outlined 16 major European airports where travellers can expect "significant" queues. Of these airports, five are directly accessible from Cardiff Airport: Tenerife South Palma de Mallorca Alicante Malaga Lanzarote Another four airports are also accessible indirectly from Cardiff: Verona Berlin Madrid Frankfurt Hahn Paris Beauvais, Milan Bergamo, Krakow, Lisbon, Madrid, Budapest, and Milan Malpensa will also be severely affected by the EES this summer, but Cardiff Airport does not offer flights to these destinations. Chief operations officer at Ryanair, Neal McMahon, said: "Families heading away for a well-earned summer holiday should be thinking about suitcases, suncream and sangria, not standing in passport queues for hours. "The reality is that the EES system isn’t working properly and families are paying the price for a system that does not work months after launch. "Passengers should not be the testing ground for unfinished border infrastructure." Mr McMahon has backed calls from EU Member States to extend current EES flexibilities into early 2027. This extension would give airports and border authorities more time to fix malfunctioning kiosks, increase staffing levels, and ensure the system can operate efficiently before full enforcement is introduced. He said: "We support calls from EU Member States to urgently extend the EES flexibilities. "This will give airports and border authorities the time to improve the infrastructure, fix the broken devices and hire more staff so that families can travel through Europe without disruption." Ryanair has advised UK passengers travelling to and from non-Schengen destinations, or transiting through affected European airports, to allow extra time for their journey and be prepared for lengthy waits at passport control. New eGate rules at Cardiff Airport Holidaymakers travelling to and from Cardiff Airport this summer will also need to be aware of new eGate rules that came into force earlier this month. Children aged eight and nine, who are at least 120cm (3ft 11in) tall and travelling with an adult, can now use UK airport eGates. The previous minimum age for eGate use was 10, and before 2023, it was 12. The change is expected to speed up arrivals, as younger children used to be processed manually by a Border Force officer. The new rule will make an estimated 1.5 million more children eligible to use eGates over the next year, based on 2025 UK arrival figures. The change applies to the 13 UK airports using eGates: London Heathrow London Gatwick London City London Luton London Stansted Manchester Birmingham Bristol East Midlands Newcastle Cardiff Edinburgh Glasgow RECOMMENDED READING: What are the Cardiff Airport liquid rules and is there still a 100ml limit? Cardiff Airport passengers warned of change that could see them denied entry to Spain A guide to Cardiff Airport - parking, drop off/pick up charges, shops and more More than 290 eGates operate across the UK, including at certain ports and European entry points where British travellers are processed. In addition, 48 EU airports now allow British holidaymakers to use eGates. These eGates are open to travellers arriving from non-Schengen countries such as the US, Australia, and Japan. https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/life.text: Imagine walking into a Louis Vuitton store while on holiday, ready to look at a few bags, only to be told by the employee to stop shopping and go outside.Thatâs pretty much what happened to Indian content creator Vagmita Singh, better known as @thatindianchick_, during her solo trip to Budapest.And the reason she was told off? The weather.Vagmita shared the funny encounter in a video, explaining that she had gone to a Louis Vuitton showroom because, well, she wanted to shop. She was looking at a few bags when an employee helping her casually asked if it was her first time in Budapest."Yeah," she told him.That seemingly harmless answer apparently changed the entire conversation.According to Vagmita, the employee was genuinely shocked."First time? Then my friend, what are you doing shopping?" she recalled him saying.Apparently, Budapest had just come through a long winter and the sun was finally out. And this employee was clearly not impressed that a first-time visitor was choosing to spend the rare sunny day inside a luxury store."After such long winter, we have sun and you are shopping? Go outside. Go outside right now," Vagmita recalled him saying.Now, most people might have been a little taken aback by being told to leave a store after walking in to shop.But Vagmita took it in exactly the way it was intended - as a hilarious, slightly unexpected piece of travel advice. "Sorry, I didn't know that I would find my dad in someone else's avatar on my solo trip," she joked.And honestly, that line probably sums up the entire interaction. The funny part? She didn't exactly follow his advice completely. Vagmita revealed that she still bought the bag."Now I'm outside. Now I'm outside," she said at the end of the video, as if reassuring the employee, and perhaps her new internet audience - that she had eventually listened.The story soon started making the rounds online, with people finding the entire exchange oddly wholesome.After all, imagine being in a luxury store and having an employee basically tell you that your money would be better spent after you've actually seen the city.Some social media users joked that the man had temporarily become Vagmita's father for the day. Others loved his reaction, saying it was a refreshing reminder that travelling isn't only about shopping or ticking off tourist attractions.And then there were the solo travellers who could relate to the experience of having random encounters with strangers that somehow become the stories you remember long after the trip is over.For Vagmita, what started as a quick shopping trip turned into one of those completely unexpected holiday moments.She got the Louis Vuitton bag she wanted. She also got a lecture about enjoying the sunshine. And, perhaps most importantly, she found a story funny enough to share with thousands of people online.So yes, she went outside. But not before buying the bag.Looking for trusted parenting advice? Follow TOI Parenting Circle on Instagram for expert guidance, relatable stories, and practical tips delivered every day.

https://www.dw.com/en/bangladesh-lawmake.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J7Re Alamgir is the secretary general of the BNP [FILE: February 14, 2026] Image: Abu Sufian Jewel/ZUMA/IMAGO Advertisement Bangladesh's parliament is set to elect the country's new president on Thursday, with the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party's (BNP) Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir widely expected to win. The BNP holds more than a two-thirds majority in parliament, making it unlikely that retired army officer-turned-politician Oli Ahmed of the opposition Jamaat-e-Islami-led alliance will get the vote. Lawmakers are set to vote at 2 p.m. local time (0800 UTC). The election comes after former president Mohammed Shahabuddin, a close ally of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina , resigned in July citing health concerns. Who is Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir? In February, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's BNP won a landslide victory in the first election since Hasina's 2024 ouster. The party is expected to use its majority to hand the 78-year-old Alamgir the largely ceremonial presidency. "I never thought that I would become the president, it is the infinite grace of the party and almighty Allah," he told reporters on Tuesday, according to the state news agency BSS. "Even after becoming president, I wish to remain beside the people and serve them." Alamgir was repeatedly arrested under Hasina's government, facing dozens of charges he said were politically motivated. He has been hailed in the media for "keeping the BNP organized and maintaining the party's political presence during difficult times," referring to Hasina's rule. Photo by Dominic Bonuccelli St. Mark's Square in the heart of Venice teems with tourists in the midday sun, but you can have it to yourself early in the morning or late at night. Photo by Dominic Bonuccelli I’ve been traveling to Venice for more than 40 years. On a recent trip to update my guidebook, I had to admit: The city felt different. While still one of Europe’s most romantic and distinctive destinations, globalization and modern life are changing Venice — for better and for worse. As I wandered Venice’s meandering streets and canalside walkways, it became obvious just how much the city has changed in recent decades. More multilingual menus featured Chinese and Korean, thanks to a huge increase in visitors from east Asia. Litter grew out the tops of garbage cans like bushy heads of hair. The tourist thoroughfares, such as the lanes between St. Mark’s Square and the Rialto Bridge, were as crowded as ever, if not moreso, but in the evening, all that bustle was completely gone. These days, a huge portion of Venetian visitors don’t spend the night, but blitz in for the day from cruise ships and cheap mainland hotels. While tourism continues to keep Venice afloat, fewer overnight guests and dinner-time restaurant customers mean that the tourist trade is no longer as lucrative for the people who still call the city home. The city has attempted to address this by charging day-trippers a €5–10 “access fee” to visit the historic center. The funds are intended to help offset the drawbacks of overtourism — but the jury’s out as to how much impact a relatively small fee can have. While midday crowds fill the streets and blockbuster sights, mornings and evenings in Venice are serene. Travelers willing to hunker down in Venice for a few days have the city to themselves in the early and late hours. Set your alarm and treat yourself to at least one walk at sunrise — it’s striking how St. Mark’s Square is an entirely different experience without the mobs. At Caffè Florian, the most venerable café on the square, the manager lamented how, over his tenure, the café’s elegance has been trampled with poorly dressed tourists (which describes me fairly well, I must admit). Still, I love this place, with its smoke-stained mirrors, white-tuxedoed waiters, and finicky piano and string quartet, which somehow gets called an “orchestra.” While you can enjoy a romantic drink here with live music and all the tourists, a quiet cup of coffee in the morning, surrounded by the patina of faded grandeur, is also a treat. In so many ways, when you get up early and stay out late, you enjoy a different (and seemingly more real) Venice. Likewise, on the vaporetto water buses, there’s a stark contrast between the midday mobs and the easygoing joy of riding at quiet times. Venice is two cities: one garishly touristy and the other so romantic and tranquil that it makes you go fortissimo in describing it. It’s not just cruise ships that are changing Venice — globalization is, too. The city has long been known for its exquisite glass, produced on the isle of Murano since 1292, when the furnaces were moved to prevent fires on the main island (and to protect the secrets of Venetian glassmaking). The island’s factories still produce ornate vases, beaded necklaces, and other goods. But these days, many glass trinkets being sold to tourists are made in China or Mexico, and it’s undercutting the economy of the local glassmakers. There’s a strong push to encourage people to buy genuine Venetian glass with the Murano seal. In this new, more diverse Venice, sometimes it seems that restaurants and market stalls are run by as many Sri Lankans and Chinese as Italians. Odds are that the strolling accordionist trolling for tips at your dinner table is Romanian. Venice’s resident population continues to drop, thanks in part to the challenges of raising a family here. Imagine living in a small, expensive apartment that occasionally floods, or pushing a stroller over arched bridges while hauling groceries. One pharmacy here hosts an electric reader board in its window that ticks down with each Venetian who moves away or dies. On my first day of my last visit it read 47,759. The next day it was 47,756. In many ways, Venice seems built for romantics. But romance isn’t what it used to be, either. It seems there aren’t even lovers on gondolas anymore — everyone seems too consumed with snapping selfies to drink in the enchanting scene. Despite all the changes, Venice still awes me with its ethereal beauty and lovely views — which can hit you from any direction (literally — always look both ways after crossing over a Venetian bridge). I know of no other place so well suited for taking a mental break from the outside world, and letting yourself be present in its otherworldly elegance. If you pause anywhere in Venice and simply observe, you’ll witness the one-of-a-kind wonder of this forever-unique city on the lagoon. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-fails.text: BRUSSELS — EU capitals failed to extend one of the bloc’s Russia sanctions schemes on Monday, five EU diplomats told POLITICO. Three of them said EU ambassadors will reconvene later Monday for further discussion. Ambassadors meeting in Brussels needed to reach unanimous agreement on Monday because the regime — which governs the asset freezes of about 3,000 individuals and companies — expires Tuesday. Slovakia has demanded that the bloc remove two rich Russian businessmen from the sanctions list: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman. France has reportedly attempted to create a compromise by suggesting only Usmanov be delisted. Most other capitals were unwilling to consider delisting anyone while Russia is firing record numbers of missiles at Ukrainian civilian targets. One of the diplomats said that “against the backdrop of rising hybrid threats and Russian drone attacks only 1 kilometer from the Polish border, it's hard to believe that France is actually asking for this.” Another part of the discussion revolves around whether to extend the measures by six months, as has been customary since 2014, or renew them for 12 months. Slovakia is understood to be unwilling to back the longer period. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dw.com/en/why-ai-researchers.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MZxq Some researchers argue that artificial general intelligence could pose unforeseeable risks Image: Marc Asensio/NurPhoto/IMAGO Advertisement Dramatic warnings about the existential risks posed by artificial intelligence to humanity are nothing new. As early as the 1940s, the renowned scientist and science fiction author Isaac Asimov explored potential risks and unintended consequences of intelligent machines. In 1991, Hollywood blockbuster "Terminator 2" imagined a dystopian 2029 in which an out-of-control military AI called Skynet directs killer robots in a war against humanity. If the warnings of several of the biggest names in AI are to be believed, a similar scenario could become a reality — even before 2029. The opening sequence of 'Terminator 2' depicts a dystopian future where AI has spiraled out of control and turned against humanity Image: Columbia/dpa/picture alliance Growing calls for strict regulation "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," AI researcher Jacob Coxon posted on X last week, without exactly explaining how it might happen. "No other human activity poses this level of danger," he added. Coxon also revealed that he had quit his job at Anthropic, a US-based AI company, in protest against what he saw as an irresponsible race among AI companies to develop an ever better, self-improving superintelligence. He warned that algorithms could begin to analyze and improve their own source code independently, which could shrink development cycles from several months to just a few minutes and thus make them uncontrollable. Coxon is not an isolated voice. Nobel Prize-winning physicist Geoffrey Hinton, often called the "Godfather of AI," has been warning for years about the serious consequences of artificial superintelligence. In 2023, he left his job at Google to publicly warn of the dangers of AI technologies he helped pioneer. Yoshua Bengio, a pioneer of artificial neural networks and deep learning, has also expressed concern about current developments and called for government regulation. As recently as July 2026, more than 1,000 employees of leading AI companies warned in an open letter of an imminent loss of control if the race for "superintelligence" were not subject to significantly stricter regulations. Caught in an unregulated race? Despite the growing warnings, US President Donald Trump's administration has clearly shifted its AI policy toward minimizing regulatory hurdles and accelerating AI development. In his X post, Jacob Coxon indirectly criticized the consequences of this policy: "At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes. At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk." Coxon, who had moved from OpenAI to Anthropic in early 2026, is familiar with both corporate cultures. In an interview with The Wall Street Journal , he said that under the "most aggressive scenarios," things could spiral out of control as early as the end of 2027. America's AI boom: Who pays the price? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for his part, is currently calling for a coordinated, industry-wide slowdown in development to buy time to address the risks and prevent any misuse of AI. In a lengthy essay shared on X over the weekend, he wrote that in six to 12 months, AI agents "could be capable ​of taking over the entire internet" and potentially cause "hundreds of billions of dollars in damage" without proper guardrails. Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said they agree with Amodei. The alignment problem In recent years, numerous experts have voiced concern about the rapid AI advances , particularly the development of artificial general intelligence, which refers to systems that not only solve individual tasks but also match or exceed human intellectual capabilities in nearly all areas. Sophisticated AI models, for instance, may pursue goals in ways that diverge from human intentions, something AI security researchers refer to as the "alignment problem." On top of that, even developers can't always fully understand how AI makes certain decisions. And so, it's no surprise that Coxon's former colleague Evan Hubinger came to his defense. "Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger, who himself is the team lead for alignment stress tests at Anthropic, wrote on X. In his post, Hubinger made clear that Anthropic hasn't yet found a solution to the alignment problem and warned that an AI model might begin to resist being shut down, because that would limit its ability to achieve its programmed goal. Exaggerated hysteria? Other AI experts, however, consider such doomsday scenarios to be extremely unlikely. Among the most prominent critics of the so-called AI doomers is Meta's chief scientist, Yann LeCun. In October 2024, he dismissed such concerns as "complete nonsense." Still, other experts note that developing AI systems requires enormous amounts of computing power, energy, data and infrastructure. They argue that an AI model cannot simply take over the world because it would need to rely on servers, power grids, communication systems and physical resources that are controlled by humans. China's humanoid robots put to the test To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Does the real danger lie elsewhere? In fact, many experts see the short-term risks not so much in the extinction of humanity as in the numerous indirect consequences of AI systems that already exist even without superintelligence. These include disinformation campaigns on an unprecedented scale and the related manipulation of democratic processes, an expansion of mass surveillance, and job losses across numerous industries. Just last week, Anthropic revealed that there had been several attempts by users to misuse its Claude AI models for research that could support biological weapons development. The company said it had banned the accounts involved. In August, Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI caused a stir when they announced that their AI systems had unintentionally carried out autonomous hacking activities . Following reports of further AI hacking attacks during testing, even top US AI frontier labs are now expressing a willingness to slow down the development of the technology. https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/s.text: Add Spokesman-Review on Google By Francesca Chambers and Miles J. Herszenhorn USA Today NEW YORK – After an explosives-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at a German airport, European leaders did something they’d stopped short of doing before: publicly blame Russia. For years they’d suspected that Russian President Vladimir Putin was behind acts of sabotage across Europe, but there was little or no evidence to prove it. But recently, Moscow is raising even more suspicions. Russian submarines have attempted to disable critical subsea cables in the Arctic. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Latvian, Lithuanian and Estonian airspace. And Polish authorities recently blamed Russia for starting a fire at a factory producing weapons for Ukraine. The aggression has marked an escalation in the standoff between NATO leaders and Putin, as the United States, Canada and Europe seek to deter Russia and support Ukraine without being dragged directly into the war. “We see them really increasing their attacks,” Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief, told USA Today. “They are testing how far they can go.” As Russia has incurred severe losses on the battlefield, Putin has stepped up his attempts to scare Ukraine’s allies out of supporting them through so-called hybrid attacks, European officials and experts say. Hybrid warfare typically refers to unconventional attacks using unmarked soldiers, sabotage and cyberwarfare. The attacks are aimed at intimidating NATO countries to pull back on assistance not only to Ukraine, said former U.S. Ambassador to Poland Daniel Fried, but also to Eastern European nations that Russia covets. “I think Putin’s instinct will be to find a space where pushing back is more difficult,” Fried said, “and the Russians have the ability to smirk and deny responsibility while everybody knows it’s them.” The attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany in August was particularly dangerous and irresponsible, officials said. If the drone had exploded, it would have caused significant damage and potentially killed civilians. German authorities said the drone components were known to them from “Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine.” Intelligence also pointed to “people being involved who acted on behalf of Russian state entities,” the country’s interior minister said. “It was very clear. I mean, the evidence was there, what happened,” Kallas said in an interview from the EU’s office near the United Nations. Putin’s history of crossing red lines Throughout his 26-year rule over Russia, Putin has found that he could challenge NATO with relative impunity. Over the years, officials have also accused Russia of meddling in elections in the United States and Europe. Intelligence agencies in Europe have blamed Russia for assassinating Putin’s enemies in countries such as the United Kingdom and Germany. Putin, who once called the collapse of the Soviet Union the “greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the century,” has long wanted to restore Russian control over former Soviet republics such as Ukraine. Months after the 2008 NATO summit in Bucharest, where the alliance committed to future membership for Georgia and Ukraine, Russia launched a war against Georgia and occupied its Abkhazia and South Ossetia regions. Shortly after a democratic uprising in Kyiv led to the ouster of Ukraine’s pro-Kremlin president in 2014, Russian forces without insignia – dubbed little green men – invaded the Crimean Peninsula. Weeks later, Putin illegally annexed Crimea and supported armed separatists groups in eastern Ukraine. “Time and again, our fear of escalation has dominated, and we have therefore undermined our own deterrent,” said Ivo Daalder, who served as U.S. ambassador to NATO in the Obama administration. “As a result, Putin has just moved further and further.” The insufficient response from the United States and Europe to the aggression laid the groundwork for Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, current and former U.S. and European officials have said. Putin believed that he would capture Kyiv within days, according to U.S. intelligence, but Russian forces have only managed to capture 12% of Ukrainian territory since the start of the full-scale invasion more than four years ago. “He totally underestimated Ukraine and also the western part of the world,” Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told USA Today. “We don’t want Putin to do this kind of miscalculation again against NATO.” U.S. concerned sabotage will lead to wider war The escalation of Russian hybrid attacks and other acts of sabotage against NATO countries comes as the Pentagon is weighing whether to significantly reduce its military presence in Europe. Meanwhile, some European countries are increasingly concerned, based on intelligence, that Russia could launch a military operation against a NATO country in an attempt to test Article 5 of the alliance’s treaty. Article 5 requires all NATO members to treat an attack against one ally as an attack against them all. The Danish government’s defense intelligence service said on Thursday, for instance, that “there is a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a Wednesday news conference that the United States is worried Russia’s war in Ukraine will spread into neighboring European countries. “Be it through a hybrid attack, be it through a sabotage attack, be it through a misunderstanding,” Rubio said, “some pilot went the wrong way, and all of a sudden we’ve got active combat.” A Russian drone struck a train on the Ukraine-Poland border earlier this month, narrowly missing a train carrying European politicians and diplomats. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz denounced the Russian hybrid attacks during a Security Council briefing on Wednesday . “We have violations of neighboring airspace, including NATO airspace, that create risks that no one in this room takes lightly,” Waltz said. “And I want to be clear that we condemn, in the strongest terms, any attempts to broaden the war.” Matthew Whitaker, the U.S. ambassador to NATO, told USA Today in an interview last month that allies should be clear-eyed and ready to confront the threat posed by Russia. Tsahkna said that NATO countries should publicly and forcefully call out the Russian acts of sabotage but added that he has seen no evidence of Moscow preparing for a large-scale military attack against Estonia or any other NATO ally while the Russian military is taking a battering in Ukraine. “We may see larger scale provocations or something more serious, but it is not about full-scale aggression. We don’t see it coming,” he said. “We cannot allow Putin to play with our fears.” Kallas said that whether Europe gets pulled into a wider war with Russia “very much depends on” the alliance’s response. If the Americans are saying very clearly that Article 5 stands, she said, then the Russians know what they are risking: full-scale war with Europe. That is why it is important that Europe continues to build up its military capabilities, Kallas said. “All the member states are investing more in defense, and at the same time, keeping the transatlantic alliance alive and sending clear messages to Russia that we will stand together in response if it goes over the threshold.” How far will Putin go? NATO nations, including the United States, have emphasized the necessity of deterrence while declining to say what would be a triggering event. After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, former President Joe Biden repeatedly warned that a direct conflict between NATO and Russia would be World War III and must be avoided at all costs. But NATO’s determination to avoid escalation is why Putin has continued to test the alliance’s limits, according to Daalder. He said that the question NATO leaders should be asking is not whether a Russian act of aggression crosses the Article 5 threshold, but how NATO will respond. “No matter what the provocation, we have been more worried that this will lead to a war than we are in sending Putin the message that we have serious red lines that we keep,” Daalder said. After Germany officially blamed Russia for the attempted drone attack, many NATO leaders issued statements of solidarity with Berlin. President Donald Trump said that “Putin is not looking to attack NATO territory.” On Sept. 18, Trump said that Russia has been “attacking Ukrainian allies for approximately five years.” Trump has sent mixed signals on Russia in just the last week. He signed into law a bill authorizing new Russian sanctions and called Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy a capable leader at the United Nations, then invited Putin to join him in Miami for a Group of 20 summit. The lack of a firm commitment from the United States to allies in Canada and Europe has only further emboldened Putin, says Roland Freudenstein, co-founder of the Brussels Freedom Hub. “Every hateful tweet by Trump on social media against the Europeans is poison for our deterrence posture vis-a-vis Putin,” Freudenstein said. For now, Tsahkna said that the European strategy to Russian hybrid attacks should be: “attribute, put more sanctions, respond.” “We are not terrorist countries,” he said. “We are not going to organize terrorist attacks in Russia as a response for these attacks or hybrid attacks, but there must be public attribution.” Francesca Chambers is a White House correspondent for USA TODAY covering foreign policy and presidential elections. You can follow her on X @fran_chambers. Miles J. Herszenhorn covers the Pentagon and world affairs for USA TODAY. You can follow him on X @mherszenhorn. https://www.bursa.ro/was-bolojan-traded-.text: A state-owned company rejects a commercial proposal it deems too risky, prompting the Minister of Energy to seek intervention from the President and the Prime Minister, citing the relationship with the United States. Approximately two months after an unfavorable assessment of the acquisition, the Ministry of Energy's Control Body arrives at the company. Subsequently, the U.S. Ambassador in Athens is alleged to have made a remark regarding Washington's capacity to change governments. Less than a month later, the PSD withdraws its ministers from the Bolojan Cabinet, and the government falls following a motion of no confidence, passed on May 5th, initiated by the PSD and AUR. This sequence of events marks the starting point of the "Guilfoyle affair." In the following lines, we aim to demonstrate the connections between these events: who was pursuing a business deal, who exerted pressure, and whether these actions influenced the political decision to oust the government in Bucharest. The scandal that erupted in late September stems from a Wall Street Journal investigation into the activities of the U.S. Ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, and her close ties to Christos Marafatsos, a lobbyist for the Greek group Aktor. The American publication describes an insistent promotion of the company's interests within the framework of U.S. energy diplomacy; however, both the Ambassador's legal counsel and representatives for Aktor have denied any impropriety. Nevertheless, the question raised by the investigation remains valid: where does the representation of a state's interests end, and where does the promotion of a private intermediary's commercial interests begin? At the heart of the controversy in Romania lies a dinner held at the U.S. Embassy in Athens. The Financial Times, citing sources present at the dinner in question, reports that on March 18, 2026, Kimberly Guilfoyle alluded to the potential collapse of the government in Bucharest, stemming from its opposition to the procurement of American liquefied natural gas (LNG) via the Greece-Bulgaria-Romania-Ukraine Vertical Corridor. The remark attributed to the ambassador, by both The Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times, is: "We can do this to any country we want. We can do it here, too" (referring to Greece). This statement is highly significant, especially considering that Kimberly Guilfoyle was appointed ambassador to Athens by the Trump administration and is the former fiancee of Donald Trump Jr., the son of the American president himself. According to accounts from these two American publications, the Greek Minister of Energy, Stavros Papastavrou, replied to Guilfoyle by stating that Washington cannot replace the elected government of Greece. If the statement was indeed made in the terms reported, it is a grave matter. It frames the ousting of an allied government as a tool available to a foreign power. However, a statement attributed to a diplomat, even when documented by major publications, does not, in itself, prove the existence of an operation to topple a cabinet. In the case of Romania, any investigation must move beyond mere statements and examine concrete documentation: commercial proposals, economic analyses, ministerial correspondence, negotiating mandates, and official oversight records. *Chronology of events along the Athens-Bucharest axis The commercial thread begins prior to the dinner in Athens. On November 7, 2025, Atlantic-SEE LNG Trade, Nova Power & Gas, and Transgaz signed a memorandum of understanding. The document, subsequently published by Antena 3 CNN, identifies the Greek firm as the seller, Nova as the buyer, and Transgas in its capacity as a transmission system operator. The plan envisaged negotiating the purchase of 20 TWh (terawatt-hours) annually for 20 years, starting in 2030. The American gas was to be regasified in Greece and then transported further via regional infrastructure. According to the cited source, the memorandum was non-binding and did not evolve into a firm commercial contract. In December 2025, Romgaz evaluated a proposal from Atlantic-SEE LNG Trade. According to a document reviewed by the website e-nergia.ro, Romgaz's management did not consider signing under the offered terms to be justified. The analysis estimates a cost of 33-42 EUR/MWh (megawatt-hour), comparing this against a TTF (free market) forward curve of 30-40 EUR/MWh for the 2030-2040 period. In unfavorable scenarios involving the relationship between American Henry Hub prices and European market prices, Romgaz's projected losses ranged from 50 million to 310 million EUR annually, depending on free-market price levels. The document leaves the door open for negotiating terms that would better protect Romgaz's interests. Consequently, Romgaz's rejection concerned the specific terms of the offer, rather than the prospect of purchasing American LNG in principle. The figure of over 300 million EUR represents a risk estimate, not an actual loss already incurred, nor an inevitable outcome for every year of the contract. Nevertheless, for a state-controlled company, such a scenario requires robust justification before entering into a commitment spanning two decades. Those who support the acquisition must demonstrate why the strategic advantages outweigh the commercial risk, under what conditions, and using whose funds. Rather than remaining strictly within the realm of commercial negotiations, the matter has ascended to the highest levels of the state. G4Media has published letters sent on January 16, 2026, by Bogdan Ivan, the Minister of Energy. to Nicuşor Dan and Ilie Bolojan, following Romgaz's refusal. The Minister proposed an intergovernmental agreement between Romania and the U.S., an explicit negotiating mandate backed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of National Defense, and the Romanian Intelligence Service, as well as seeking the approval of the Supreme Council of National Defense (CSAT) and informing the European Commission. The key factor that shifts the weight of the entire undertaking is the stated need to avoid the "risk of a diplomatic impasse with our strategic partner, the U.S.," according to Social Democrat Bogdan Ivan. The letter also pointed to the prospect of structural gas deficits beginning in 2036. The letter suggests that a disagreement regarding the advisability of a commercial offer is being framed as a potential diplomatic issue; however, it remains unclear who exactly signaled such an impasse or what concrete consequences it might entail. Was this a warning received by the Minister of Energy, or was it his own assessment? Was there any official communication from the American side? Furthermore, what obligation could possibly fall upon the Romanian state as a result of a non-binding memorandum between companies? *Refusal during a teleconference, followed by an inspection by the Control Body On February 11, 2026, Bogdan Ivan, in his capacity as Minister of Energy, held a teleconference with representatives from Romgaz and Transgaz. According to HotNews, citing several sources, Ivan attempted to persuade Romgaz to purchase American LNG through Greek and Romanian intermediaries. Some HotNews sources characterize this situation and Ivan's intervention as pressure exerted on the state-owned company. Romgaz representatives explained to HotNews that an assessment of the proposal's viability did not provide an economic justification for initiating or approving the operation; furthermore, the company issued a press release stating that no political pressure had been exerted upon it. Nevertheless, on February 24, representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs signed an energy declaration in Washington, which they described as political in nature, without disclosing the memorandum requested by the media. Prior to this declaration, on February 16, 2026, the Ministry of Energy's Control Body began an inspection at Romgaz, focused on the status of the investment project at Iernut. The Ministry confirmed the inspection, noting that the resulting report was undergoing internal review and approval procedures. Consequently, the inspection commenced approximately two months after the unfavorable assessment in December and five days after the teleconference on February 11. While the close timing of these events invites questions, it does not in itself prove that pressure was exerted by the Ministry. Officially, the Iernut project was the stated subject of the inspection, and delays in a public project can constitute a legitimate basis for such an inquiry. *The Bucharest dinner and the PSD's withdrawal from Government On March 31, 2026, just 13 days after the dinner in Athens where Kimberly Guilfoyle made remarks regarding what the U.S. is capable of doing in any nation, including Greece, she was photographed at a restaurant in Bucharest alongside PSD president Sorin Grindeanu, Minister of Energy Bogdan Ivan, presidential advisor Florin Vlădică, and others. On April 23, the PSD ministers resigned from the Bolojan government, and on May 5, the entire Cabinet was dismissed following the Parliament's adoption of a censure motion initiated by the PSD and AUR, and supported in the legislature by the other sovereignist parties - SOS, POT, PACE, and UPR. The Spanish daily El País notes this sequence of events and the parliamentary support provided by the PSD and AUR for the dismissal, while also specifying that reports regarding the conversation in Athens do not provide sufficient public evidence to conclude that Washington orchestrated the fall of the executive in Bucharest. On July 7, 2026, Kimberly Guilfoyle was in Mykonos, according to a report by ProTV on October 2, which cites Greek media and Instagram posts. There, she met with the U.S. Ambassador to Belgium, Bill White, and a group that included businessman Adam Kidan, a close associate of Donald Trump, as well as Ethan Cohen. The following day, July 8, a group arrived on the island via private jet, including Victor Ponta; Florin Manole, former Minister of Labor in the Bolojan Cabinet and current Minister of Labor in the Niculescu government; Mihai Daraban, President of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Romania (CCIR); Cristian Deliorga and several businesspeople. According to a statement given by Mihai Daraban to ProTV, the Romanian politicians held discussions with American investors interested in the energy, agriculture, and rail transport sectors. The head of the CCIR declined to disclose their identities, citing the investors' opposition to doing so. He, along with Ponta and Manole, denied having met with Guilfoyle. It should be noted that on September 28, Romgaz published a statement on the Bucharest Stock Exchange website asserting that "no Romanian state official has exerted pressure” on the company. It further clarifies that commercial decisions are determined by the company's internal corporate mechanisms and are based on economic, commercial, and strategic feasibility. Although the state holds 70% of the capital, this status does not override governance rules or the rights of other shareholders, the document states. This denial is explicit and must be recorded as the official position of the company's management. Also on September 28, Sorin Grindeanu denied having discussed gas contracts with Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle, stating that their conversation in late March focused on Romania's role as a transit country for the Vertical Gas Corridor. The PSD leader rejected the notion of American involvement in the dismissal of the Bolojan cabinet; however, notably, he characterized the Bolojan administration as "the most anti-American government in Romania's post-1989 history.” He even voiced this sentiment from the parliamentary rostrum during the session in which the government proposed by Siegfried Mureşan was rejected. This label shifts the dispute from the realm of accounting to that of geopolitics. If reservations regarding a specific contract contribute to a verdict of "anti-Americanism,” the reasoning behind this must be explained. A strategic partnership implies shared interests, but it also entails the right to negotiate and to reject unfavorable terms. Otherwise, an economic assessment becomes suspect simply because it fails to yield the outcome desired by one of the partners. *Missing explanations For his part, Bogdan Ivan rejects any link between the discussions on energy and the removal of the Prime Minister, maintaining that he had requested a written mandate from the Government, which he never received before leaving office. Bogdan Ivan states that the discussions during the dinner with Kimberly Guilfoyle concerned the "Vertical Corridor" and points to the potential for LNG contracts priced at approximately euro27/MWh, as well as additional annual profits of around euro250 million for Transgaz. Transgaz's press releases provide an important point of reference. In the release dated November 7, 2025, the company outlines capacity products for transport toward Ukraine, coordinated tariff reductions of 25-50%, and the prospect of increasing capacity at the Negru Vodă-Kardam interconnection point from 5.03 to 9.41 billion cubic meters per year. Ion Sterian, the company's CEO, notes in the same release that Romania has been promoting the "Vertical Corridor" concept since 2016. The document addresses infrastructure and its utilization, including for LNG and gas from the Caspian region. The project continued even after Romgaz declined to participate. A press release from July 15, 2026, describes preparations to extend the Vertical Corridor toward Serbia and North Macedonia, emphasizing the need to enhance its commercial appeal including through adjustments to the tariff structure. On September 4, the extension into the Western Balkans was formalized via a new memorandum, signed in the presence of Kimberly Guilfoyle and regional officials. Furthermore, Transgaz announced a memorandum signed on August 6 with Argent LNG, concerning the exploration of an investment in the American company, which is developing a terminal in Louisiana. The framework is non-binding, the planned capacity is 25 million tonnes per year, and the first shipment is scheduled for 2030. This is a project distinct from the Atlantic-SEE LNG Trade proposal. Its existence demonstrates that rejecting the terms of a specific transaction does not equate to ending energy cooperation with the U.S. *From the request for a hearing in Congress to a resignation The revelations also triggered oversight by the U.S. Congress. On October 1, 2026, Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democratic member of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, demanded an explanation from Secretary of State Marco Rubio and called for the ambassador's removal should the allegations be confirmed. In a statement on October 10, Meeks announced that he had requested an immediate investigation by the State Department's Office of Inspector General; in a separate letter, he also demanded that Guilfoyle provide testimony under oath before the committee. The inquiry concerned her dealings with a foreign company and a political donor, a lobbyist's access to official meetings, the use of private flights, and an alleged solicitation of funds to cover a personal debt. Over the course of about two weeks in early October, the succession of revelations and political reactions rapidly eroded Kimberly Guilfoyle's credibility. The Wall Street Journal supplemented the allegations regarding energy diplomacy with reports that she had asked a donor, Eric Deters, to settle a $100,000 debt in exchange for access to administration officials. Deters stated that he did not pay the amount. The ambassador's legal counsel contested the accusations, asserting tha
